questions.question: A square patio is covered with 144 equal square tiles, and all 144 tiles are used to make one big square with the same number of rows as columns. How many tiles are along one side?
questions.explain: A square root asks which number times itself gives the area, so look for n x n = 144; since 12 x 12 = 144, one side has 12 tiles. The trap is halving: 72 is 144 divided by 2, and 72 x 72 is far bigger than 144.

questions.question: A square art board is divided into 169 equal small squares (13 rows of 13). A shaded block inside it is itself a square made of exactly 16 of those small squares, so the shaded part is 16/169 of the whole board. What is the value of the square root of 16/169?
questions.explain: Take the square root of the numerator and the denominator separately: the root of 16 is 4 and the root of 169 is 13, giving 4/13. The trap is rooting only one part and leaving 4/169 or 16/13.

questions.question: A community centre lobby is tiled with 400 equal square tiles arranged in one large square, with the same number of tiles in each row as in each column. How many tiles are in one row?
questions.explain: Ask which number multiplied by itself gives 400: 20 x 20 = 400, so each row has 20 tiles. The trap is treating the radical sign as dividing by 2, which gives 200 and would make a square of 40 000 tiles.

questions.question: A square school banner is divided into 100 equal small squares (10 rows of 10). A logo covers a smaller square block made of exactly 9 of those squares, so the logo covers 9/100 of the banner. What is the square root of 9/100?
questions.explain: Root the top and the bottom: the root of 9 is 3 and the root of 100 is 10, so the answer is 3/10, and 3/10 x 3/10 = 9/100 checks it. The trap is rooting only one part, which leaves 9/10 or 3/100.

questions.question: What is the square root of 256?
questions.explain: Find the number that multiplies by itself to give 256: 16 x 16 = 256. The trap is halving, since 128 is just 256 divided by 2 and 128 x 128 is much larger than 256.

questions.question: Mateo builds a square planter box for his balcony in Kelowna. The square base has an area of 196 square centimetres. How long is one side of the base?
questions.explain: Side length is the square root of the area, and 14 x 14 = 196, so the side is 14 cm. The trap is dividing the area by 2 to get 98, but 98 x 98 is nowhere near 196.

questions.question: Find the square root of 36/169.
questions.explain: Root the numerator and the denominator separately: the root of 36 is 6 and the root of 169 is 13, so the answer is 6/13. The trap is rooting only one part of the fraction, which gives 36/13 or 6/169.

questions.question: A square section of a gym floor in Surrey is marked off for badminton warm-ups. It has an area of 121 square metres. What is the perimeter of that square section?
questions.explain: First take the square root of the area to get the side, 11 m, then multiply by 4 to get a perimeter of 44 m. The trap is stopping at 11 m, which is only the side length.

questions.question: Priya works out the square root of 25/144 and writes 5/144. Which choice gives the correct value with the correct reason?
options: 5/12, because the root applies to top and bottom
25/12, because only the denominator gets a root
5/72, because 144 is halved to undo squaring
5/144, because only the numerator gets a root
questions.explain: A square root of a fraction acts on both parts, so the root of 25 is 5 and the root of 144 is 12, giving 5/12, and 5/12 x 5/12 = 25/144. The trap is leaving one part untouched, as in 5/144.

questions.question: Two square storage bins sit in a Victoria classroom. The smaller bin has a square base with an area of 169 square centimetres, and the larger bin has a square base with an area of 400 square centimetres. How much longer is one side of the larger base than one side of the smaller base?
questions.explain: Take each square root first, 13 cm and 20 cm, then subtract to get 7 cm. The trap is subtracting the areas to get 231, since areas cannot be compared as lengths.

questions.question: A square poster for a Vancouver science fair has an area of 9/25 of a square metre. The student wants to run a ribbon all the way around the outside edge. How many metres of ribbon are needed?
questions.explain: Root both parts to get a side of 3/5 m, then multiply by 4 for a perimeter of 12/5 m, or 2.4 m. The trap is rooting only the denominator, which turns the side into 9/5 m and inflates the answer.

questions.question: Owen says that the square root of 64 is 32, because he thinks the radical sign tells you to split the number in half. Which choice corrects him?
options: Root of 64 is 32, because half of 64 is 32
Root of 64 is 16, because 64 divided by 4 is 16
Root of 64 is 4, because 4 x 4 x 4 is 64
Root of 64 is 8, because 8 times 8 makes 64
questions.explain: A square root undoes squaring, so you need the number that multiplies by itself to give 64, and 8 x 8 = 64. The trap is halving: 32 x 32 = 1024, not 64.
